title.en: The Bronze Men from the Sea: The Oracle That Crowned Psammetichos
title.zh: 海上銅人：加冕普薩美提科斯之神諭

region.en: Buto, Nile Delta, Egypt (the most truthful oracle of Egypt, in the city of Leto)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布托（雷托城中，全埃及最靈驗之神諭）

texts.period: Oracle-fulfilment set in the 26th Dynasty (c. 664 BCE); recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.152 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, sec. 152

summary.en: Eleven kings strip Psammetichos of his power and drive him to the fen-country — because, having no golden cup, he poured his libation from a bronze helmet, fulfilling the oracle; from Buto, Egypt's most truthful oracle, comes the promise: 'vengeance would come when men of bronze appeared from the sea'; and when Ionians and Carians in bronze armour land from a plunder cruise, Psammetichos befriends them, overthrows the eleven, and makes himself king of all Egypt.
summary.zh: 十一王奪普薩美提科斯之權而逐之於沼澤——因其無金盂，乃以銅盔奠酒，適應神諭；布托（全埃及最靈之神諭）許之：『及海上銅人出，復仇必至』——既而衣銅甲之伊奧尼亞與卡里亞人因劫掠漂至，普薩美提科斯與之善，遂傾十一王而王全埃及。

sensitivity.note: Ancient oracle-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now the twelve kings continued to rule justly, but in course of time it happened thus: — After sacrifice in the temple of Hephaistos they were about to make libation on the last day of the feast, and the chief-priest, in bringing out for them the golden cups with which they had been wont to pour libations, missed his reckoning and brought eleven only for the twelve kings. Then that one of them who was standing last in order, namely Psammetichos, since he had no cup took off from his head his helmet, which was of bronze, and having held it out to receive the wine he proceeded to make libation: likewise all the other kings were wont to wear helmets and they happened to have them then.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.151.

passages.text: They taking note of that which had been done by Psammetichos and of the oracle, namely how it had been declared to them that whosoever of them should make libation with a bronze cup should be sole king of Egypt, recollecting, I say, the saying of the Oracle, they did not indeed deem it right to slay Psammetichos, since they found by examination that he had not done it with any forethought, but they determined to strip him of almost all his power and to drive him away into the fen-country.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.151.

passages.text: When he had sent to the Oracle of Leto in the city of Buto, where the Egyptians have their most truthful Oracle, there was given to him the reply that vengeance would come when men of bronze appeared from the sea. And he was strongly disposed not to believe that bronze men would come to help him; but after no long time had passed, certain Ionians and Carians who had sailed forth for plunder were compelled to come to shore in Egypt, and they having landed and being clad in bronze armour, one of the Egyptians, not having before seen men clad in bronze armour, came to the fen-land and brought a report to Psammetichos that bronze men had come from the sea and were plundering the plain. So he, perceiving that the saying of the Oracle was coming to pass, dealt in a friendly manner with the Ionians and Carians... and with the help of those Egyptians who favoured his cause and of these foreign mercenaries he overthrew the kings.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.152.

title.en: The Lake of Moiris: Two Pyramids Rising from the Water

region.en: The Fayum, Egypt (the artificial lake beside the labyrinth)
region.zh: 埃及法尤姆（迷宮旁之人工湖）

texts.period: Works of the kings of the 12th Dynasty; recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.149-150 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 149-150

summary.en: A greater marvel than the labyrinth itself: the lake of Moiris, 3,600 furlongs in circuit, fifty fathoms deep, formed by digging, 'for about in the middle of the lake stand two pyramids, each rising above the water to a height of fifty fathoms, the part which is built below the water being of just the same height; and upon each is placed a colossal statue of stone sitting upon a chair' — its water brought by canal from the Nile, flowing in six months and out six months.
summary.zh: 較迷宮更奇者乃莫伊里斯之湖：周三千六百弗隆，深五十噚，掘地而成——『湖心立二金字塔，各高出水面五十噚，其沒於水下者亦等高；塔頂各置坐於椅上之巨大石像』——湖水由運河引自尼羅，六月入湖、六月還河。

sensitivity.note: Ancient engineering-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Such is this labyrinth; but a cause for marvel even greater than this is afforded by the lake, which is called the lake of Moiris, along the side of which this labyrinth is built. The measure of its circuit is three thousand six hundred furlongs (being sixty schoines), and this is the same number of furlongs as the extent of Egypt itself along the sea. The lake lies extended lengthwise from North to South, and in depth where it is deepest it is fifty fathoms. That this lake is artificial and formed by digging is self-evident, for about in the middle of the lake stand two pyramids, each rising above the water to a height of fifty fathoms, the part which is built below the water being of just the same height; and upon each is placed a colossal statue of stone sitting upon a chair.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.149.

passages.text: The water in the lake does not come from the place where it is, for the country there is very deficient in water, but it has been brought thither from the Nile by a canal: and for six months the water flows into the lake, and for six months out into the Nile again.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.149.

title.en: Bekos: The Experiment That Dated the Nations
title.zh: 『貝科斯』：為萬民定先後之試驗

region.en: The flock-pastures of King Psammetichos, Egypt
region.zh: 埃及普薩美提科斯王之牧場

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.2 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 2

summary.en: The first recorded experiment in history: the Egyptians held they were the first of all men, until Psammetichos, 'desiring to know what men had come into being first', gave two new-born children to a shepherd with orders that no word be uttered in their presence; after two years the children cried bekos — bread, in Phrygian — 'and in this manner... the Egyptians were brought to allow that the Phrygians were a more ancient people than themselves.'
summary.zh: 史上首載之實驗：埃及人自謂為萬民之首；普薩美提科斯『欲知何族最先』，乃以二新生嬰兒付牧者，囑其前不得有一言——二歲之後，二兒呼『貝科斯』（弗呂吉亞語『麵包』）——『埃及人遂承認弗呂吉亞人先於己。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient pseudo-experiment tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now the Egyptians, before the time when Psammetichos became king over them, were wont to suppose that they had come into being first of all men; but since the time when Psammetichos having become king desired to know what men had come into being first, they suppose that the Phrygians came into being before themselves, but they themselves before all other men. Now Psammetichos, when he was not able by inquiry to find out any means of knowing who had come into being first of all men, contrived a device of the following kind: — Taking two new-born children belonging to persons of the common sort he gave them to a shepherd to bring up at the place where his flocks were, with a manner of bringing up such as I shall say, charging him namely that no man should utter any word in their presence.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.2.

passages.text: And accordingly so it came to pass; for after a space of two years had gone by, during which the shepherd went on acting so, at length, when he opened the door and entered, both the children fell before him in entreaty and uttered the word bekos, stretching forth their hands. At first when he heard this the shepherd kept silence; but since this word was often repeated... at last he declared the matter to his master. Then Psammetichos having himself also heard it, began to inquire about what nation of men named anything bekos, and inquiring he found that the Phrygians had this name for bread. In this manner and guided by an indication such as this, the Egyptians were brought to allow that the Phrygians were a more ancient people than themselves.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.2.

title.en: The Shepherd Kings: They Ruled 'Not Knowing Ra'

region.en: Avaris, eastern Delta, Egypt (the Hyksos fortress with its garrison of 240,000)
region.zh: 埃及東三角洲阿瓦里斯（牧人王之堡，守軍二十四萬）

texts.period: Hyksos rule of the 15th-16th Dynasties (c. 1650-1550 BCE); retold in D. A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913)

source.archive: Global Grey Ebooks (public domain facsimile of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend)
source.work: Donald A. Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XX, 'The Hyksos and Their Strange God'

summary.en: The age Egypt tried to forget: the invaders 'were a people of ignoble race who had confidence to invade our country, which they subdued easily without having to fight a battle. They set our towns on fire; they destroyed the temples of the gods' — called Hyksos, 'Shepherd Kings'; they fortified Avaris with a garrison of 240,000 men, and Hatshepsut could still declare: 'Since the Asiatics were in Avaris of the north land... they governed, not knowing Ra.'
summary.zh: 埃及欲忘之世：入侵者『乃卑賤之族，竟敢犯吾國，不戰而易取之；焚吾城，毀諸神之廟』——號曰希克索斯，『牧人之王』；築阿瓦里斯堡，屯軍二十四萬；至哈特謝普蘇特猶能誦曰：『亞細亞人居北國之阿瓦里斯……彼等治而不識拉。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient memory of foreign rule retold in Mackenzie 1913; passages verbatim from the retelling.

passages.text: Josephus, the patriotic Jewish historian, who believed that the Hyksos were 'the children of Israel', quoted Manetho as saying that 'they were a people of ignoble race who had confidence to invade our country, which they subdued easily without having to fight a battle. They set our towns on fire; they destroyed the temples of the gods, and caused the people to suffer every kind of barbarity. During the entire period of their dynasty they waged war against the people of Egypt, desiring to exterminate the whole race. The foreigners were called Hyksos, which signifies Shepherd Kings.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie, Egyptian Myth and Legend (1913), ch. XX, quoting Manetho via Josephus.

passages.text: Manetho's reference to a carnival of destruction is confirmed by the inscription of Queen Hatshepsut of the Eighteenth Dynasty, who declared with characteristic piety: I have restored what was cast down, I have built up what was uncompleted, Since the Asiatics were in Avaris of the north land, And the barbarians were among them, destroying buildings, While they governed, not knowing Ra.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XX.

passages.text: The Hyksos overwhelmed the land at the close of the Fourteenth Dynasty. Then they chose for a king 'one of their own people'. According to Manetho his name was Salatis... He selected Memphis as his capital, and there 'he made Upper and Lower Egypt pay tribute', while he left garrisons at places which were 'considered to be proper for them'... the foreigners erected a strongly fortified town called Avaris — afterwards destroyed by the Egyptians — and there they kept a garrison of 240,000 men.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Mackenzie (1913), ch. XX.

title.en: Thoth, Heart and Tongue of the Creator: Author of the Book of the Dead
title.zh: 托特：造主之心與舌，《亡靈書》之作者

region.en: Egypt, all periods (Thoth as the Recording Angel of the gods)
region.zh: 埃及歷代（托特為諸神之錄天使）

texts.period: Doctrine from the 1st Dynasty onward (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901, ch. IV)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. IV, 'Thoth, the Author of the Book of the Dead'

summary.en: The theology of the scribe-god: Thoth was the heart and mind of the Creator, 'and he at all times voiced the will of the great god, and spoke the words which commanded every being and thing in heaven and in earth to come into existence' — his words almighty and once uttered never without effect; he framed the laws, ordered the courses of sun, moon and stars, invented writing and mathematics, kept the celestial register as the 'Recording Angel', and as weigher of words and deeds became 'more powerful in the Other World than Osiris himself'.
summary.zh: 書吏之神之神學：托特為造主之心與智，『恆述大神之意，發言而令天地萬有皆得生成』——其言無所不能，一出而不虛；彼立天之律法、序日月星辰之行，創繪畫文字與數學，掌天界登記而為『錄天使』；司權衡言行，其判不移，遂於冥界之力『凌駕奧西里斯本人之上』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient doctrine via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Thoth was also the 'tongue' of the Creator, and he at all times voiced the will of the great god, and spoke the words which commanded every being and thing in heaven and in earth to come into existence. His words were almighty and once uttered never remained without effect. He framed the laws by which heaven, earth and all the heavenly bodies are maintained; he ordered the courses of the sun, moon, and stars; he invented drawing and design and the arts, the letters of the alphabet and the art of writing, and the science of mathematics.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. IV.

passages.text: At a very early period he was called the 'scribe (or secretary) of the Great Company of the Gods,' and as he kept the celestial register of the words and deeds of men, he was regarded by many generations of Egyptians as the 'Recording Angel.' He was the inventor of physical and moral Law and became the personification of JUSTICE; and as the Companies of the Gods of Heaven, and Earth, and the Other World appointed him to 'weigh the words and deeds' of men, and his verdicts were unalterable, he became more powerful in the Other World than Osiris himself.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. IV.

passages.text: Osiris owed his triumph over Set in the Great Judgment Hall of the Gods entirely to the skill of Thoth of the 'wise mouth' as an Advocate, and to his influence with the gods in heaven. And every follower of Osiris relied upon the advocacy of Thoth to secure his acquittal on the Day of Judgment, and to procure for him an everlasting habitation in the Kingdom of Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. IV.

title.en: Why the Body Must Be Kept Whole: Thoth's Protection of the Mummy
title.zh: 身何以必全：托特護木乃伊

region.en: Egyptian tombs, from predynastic graves to the rock chambers
region.zh: 埃及陵墓（自前王朝至巖窟墓室）

texts.period: Funerary doctrine attested from the 1st Dynasty (Budge, The Book of the Dead, 1901, ch. II)

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. II, 'The Preservation of the Mummified Body in the Tomb by Thoth'

summary.en: The theology of embalming in one paragraph: dynastic Egyptians 'attached supreme importance to the preservation and integrity of the dead body... and then sealed it up in a coffin... in a chamber hewn in the bowels of the mountain' — but the enemies of the dead were not only worms and beetles: both mummy and the spiritual elements had to be protected 'from a multitude of devils and fiends, and from the powers of darkness generally', whose road lay along the way of the dead — so Thoth's spells were set around them, even as the sun god himself owed his continued existence to a secret name Thoth provided against Aapep.
summary.zh: 防腐神學一言以蔽之：王朝埃及人『以保全亡身之完整為至要』——以香料香脂防腐，裹以百碼亞麻，封於棺槨，藏於巖腹之室——然亡者之敵非止蛆蟲甲蟲：木乃伊與寓於其身之靈素，皆須防『群魔與暗界諸力』——其途正沿亡者之路——故以托特之咒護之，如日神賴托特所授秘名以抗阿波菲斯而得永存。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary doctrine via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The dynastic Egyptians, either as the result of a difference in religious belief, or under the influence of invaders who had settled in their country, attached supreme importance to the preservation and integrity of the dead body, and they adopted every means known to them to prevent its dismemberment and decay. They cleansed it and embalmed it with drugs, spices and balsams; they anointed it with aromatic oils and preservative fluids; they swathed it in hundreds of yards of linen bandages; and then they sealed it up in a coffin or sarcophagus, which they laid in a chamber hewn in the bowels of the mountain.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. II.

passages.text: But these were not the only enemies of the dead against which precautions had to be taken, for both the mummified body and the spiritual elements which had inhabited it upon earth had to be protected from a multitude of devils and fiends, and from the powers of darkness generally. These powers of evil had hideous and terrifying shapes and forms, and their haunts were well known, for they infested the region through which the road of the dead lay when passing from this world to the Kingdom of Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. II.

passages.text: In fact it was believed in very early times in Egypt that Ra the Sun-god owed his continued existence to the possession of a secret name with which Thoth had provided him. And each morning the rising sun was menaced by a fearful monster called Aapep, which lay hidden under the place of sunrise waiting to swallow up the solar disk. It was impossible, even for the Sun-god, to destroy this 'Great Devil,' but by reciting each morning the powerful spell with which Thoth had provided him he was able to paralyse all Aapep's limbs and to rise upon this world.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. II.
